findings.title: tempfile.mkstemp sits outside the try, so a failed file write still returns a 500
findings.problem: `fd, tmp_path = tempfile.mkstemp(dir=path.parent, suffix=".tmp")` runs before the `try:`, so the `except OSError` never covers it. The function's docstring and the D-17 comments say a file-write failure must not be fatal. But common failures happen right at mkstemp: a read-only config volume, a full disk, a permission error, or a missing config dir (`_runtime_config_dir` at routes.py:97-99 returns `Path(config_path).parent`). That OSError travels through `run_in_executor` into `reset_request_post` (routes.py ~1698), which has no handler, so the request ends in an unhandled 500. The token has already been minted, stored in app.state and logged by then, but the operator gets an error page instead of the neutral confirmation. Every later request within 15 minutes hits the live-token no-op branch, so there is no retry and no second chance to write the file.
findings.fix_hint: move mkstemp inside the try (initialise tmp_path=None and skip unlink when it is None), so OSError from mkstemp is logged and not re-raised as D-17 intends
findings.why_it_matters: The promised 'file write is non-fatal' behaviour fails in exactly the read-only or misconfigured volume case it was written for, and the user sees a 500.

members.title: raw fd from mkstemp leaks if os.fchmod raises before fdopen takes ownership
members.problem: `os.fchmod(fd, 0o600)` operates on the bare fd from mkstemp before `os.fdopen` wraps it in the following `with` statement. If fchmod itself raises OSError, execution jumps to `except OSError`, which unlinks tmp_path but never closes the integer fd — fdopen (the only thing that would close it via the `with`) never ran.
source_window: # is already 0600 after os.replace with no post-rename chmod window.
members.why_it_matters: A leaked fd is an OS-level resource leak that is not freed until process exit; repeated failures (e.g. a persistently unwritable config volume being hit by repeated reset requests) would leak one fd per attempt and could eventually exhaust the process's descriptor limit.
members.fix_hint: wrap the fchmod call so fd is explicitly closed on failure before re-entering the except branch, e.g. try/except around fchmod that os.close(fd) then re-raises, or set permissions via mkstemp's mode handling instead

members.title: tempfile.mkstemp sits outside the try, so a write-permission failure returns 500 instead of the promised non-fatal path
members.problem: _write_reset_token_file calls `fd, tmp_path = tempfile.mkstemp(dir=path.parent, ...)` before the `try:`. If the config dir cannot be written (PUID/PGID mismatch, read-only mount, out of inodes), mkstemp raises an uncaught OSError. That error passes through run_in_executor and out of reset_request_post, so the user gets an unhandled 500. This contradicts D-17 ('file write is non-fatal') and the function's own docstring. The token is already minted and logged, and the next request within 15 min hits the H1 no-op path, so recovery still works. The user-visible result is still a 500 page instead of the neutral confirmation. Separately, if os.fchmod(fd) raises, the raw fd is never closed because os.fdopen has not taken it over yet. That leaks a file descriptor.
members.why_it_matters: The endpoint's stated guarantee that a file write failure never fails the request is broken on a plausible Docker volume-permission misconfiguration.
members.fix_hint: Move mkstemp inside the try. Track whether fdopen has taken over the fd, and close the raw fd in the error path if it has not.

findings.title: File descriptor leaks if os.fchmod raises before os.fdopen takes ownership
findings.problem: The raw fd from mkstemp only gets closed once `os.fdopen(fd, "w")` wraps it in the `with` block. If `os.fchmod(fd, 0o600)` raises OSError (for example EPERM on some bind-mounted or network filesystems), the except branch unlinks tmp_path, but nothing calls `os.close(fd)`, and the `finally` only closes dir_fd. The full acquire-to-release scope is in the hunk.
findings.fix_hint: close fd in the except/finally path when fdopen has not taken ownership (track a flag, or call fdopen first and fchmod via f.fileno())
findings.why_it_matters: Each failed reset request on such a filesystem leaks one descriptor in a long-running daemon.

findings.title: Fourth hand-copied atomic tempfile+fsync+replace+dir-fsync write block instead of a shared helper
findings.problem: _write_reset_token_file is a near-copy of the same atomic write sequence (mkstemp in the parent dir, fdopen, flush and fsync, os.replace, a `renamed` flag, dir fsync, warning-after-rename or error-plus-unlink-and-cleanup-error log, close dir_fd in finally). Three copies already exist: triggarr/config.py:95 `_atomic_toml_write`, triggarr/config.py:231 `generate_default_config`, and triggarr/state.py:185 `save_state`. That makes four in total, which crosses the rule-of-three threshold. The two differences are deliberate (fchmod 0600 on the temp fd, and no re-raise per D-17), and both could be parameters (mode, raise_on_error) of one shared helper. The docstring already admits it 'Mirrors _atomic_toml_write'.

findings.title: Password reset token logged in cleartext via logger.warning
findings.problem: The newly minted CSPRNG reset token is passed directly into a `logger.warning(...)` call, which per the project's own Loguru redacting-sink convention and CLAUDE.md's absolute rule ('Never log sensitive data: passwords, tokens, PII, auth headers') should never happen. The code comments acknowledge this is deliberate and that the token is intentionally excluded from `collect_secrets`/the redacting sink so it reaches 'docker logs' in the clear.
findings.current_code:
logger.warning(
    "Password reset token minted. Read from 'docker logs' or reset-token.txt: {token}",
    token=token,
)
findings.why_it_matters: The reset token grants full admin-account takeover for 15 minutes once minted. Docker logs are commonly shipped to centralized logging/aggregation systems (journald, syslog drivers, CloudWatch, Loki, etc.) that retain entries far longer than the token's 900-second validity window and may be visible to parties (other operators, support staff, log-platform admins) who should not have password-reset capability. This is a direct, acknowledged exception to the project's established secret-redaction discipline rather than an accidental leak, but it still creates a durable, lower-trust-boundary copy of a high-value credential.

members.title: Reset token reaches HTTP responses through the in-app log viewer, so anyone holding the API key can take over the password
members.problem: The new logger.warning line puts the reset token in the log message, and the token is deliberately left out of collect_secrets. setup_logging() adds a second sink, buffer_sink (triggarr/logging.py:72-84). It redacts only the values in `secrets` and then calls log_buffer.add(). That buffer is rendered over HTTP by the dashboard (routes.py:382, log_buffer.get_recent(30)) and by partial_log_viewer (routes.py:1080-1083). Both routes accept an X-Api-Key request (middleware.py:150-154) as well as a session. So the docstring's promise that the token never appears in any HTTP response body does not hold. An API-key holder can POST /reset/request (open to anyone, middleware.py:118), then GET the log viewer partial with X-Api-Key and read the token. With the token they can reset the UI password, which locks the operator out. The API key, often shared with *arr integrations or scripts, becomes a password-takeover credential. The same applies to any viewer of the dashboard log rail.

findings.title: Token-file creation errors escape the non-fatal recovery path
findings.problem: If the config volume is read-only, unwritable, or full, tempfile.mkstemp raises OSError before entering the try block. The exception propagates through the awaited executor call, causing POST /reset/request to return HTTP 500 after minting the token and recording the rate limit. The operator receives neither the neutral confirmation nor its recovery instructions, despite the token being available in logs. This contradicts the explicitly intended non-fatal handling of file-write failures.

members.problem: `fd, tmp_path = tempfile.mkstemp(dir=path.parent, suffix=".tmp")` executes before the `try:` on the next line, so any OSError it raises (missing/unwritable config dir, ENOSPC, EMFILE) propagates straight out of `_write_reset_token_file` instead of being caught by the `except OSError` handler immediately below it.

members.why_it_matters: The function's own docstring and the D-17 contract it documents guarantee the file write is non-fatal and the in-memory token stays authoritative. Since this function is invoked via run_in_executor and awaited in reset_request_post with no surrounding try/except, an OSError from mkstemp turns a documented no-op fallback into an unhandled exception in the request path — exactly the failure mode (unwritable/missing config volume) the rest of the function was written to tolerate.
